newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Insurer GAN jumps on rescue plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Insurer GAN jumps on rescue plan.

text.p: Shares in French insurer Groupe GAN soared on Friday as investors bet the French government's 20 billion franc ($3.5 billion) rescue of the state-controlled insurer would return it to profit and make it a tempting bid target.
The share jumped 21 percent to 150 francs before being suspended for the day as financial analysts switched their recommendations to "buy" from "sell".
Several attempts to requote the shares were abandoned after they repeatedly surged through price barriers, triggering a halt in trading.
"The market is betting that cleaned up of its property problems and losses, GAN will be profitable again," said an insurance analyst in Paris.

Groupe des Assurances Nationales (GAN) has run up huge losses in recent years on property loans and insurance underwriting. The bailout is the latest in a string of expensive state mop-up operations in France's financial sector.
The group said on Thursday it expected to announce a five billion franc loss for 1996 after a 1.78 billion loss in 1995. But analysts said they were pencilling in profits for 1997.
"The government is pretty much writing out a blank cheque," one London analyst said. "It's philanthropy...which, given the extent of the bailout, seems surprising."

But while expensive, GAN's rescue was not expected to prove as costly as the salvage of state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais, whose 1980s lending misadventures could land taxpayers with a bill of more than 100 billion francs.
Underpinning the share price rise, an analyst said, was the assumption that GAN, shorn of its property troubles, would be a palatable bid target.
"The market thinks after its restructuring GAN will only have its healthy assets...that would make it a tempting target for a predator," the analyst said.

The government said it planned to privatise GAN and CIC, the regional banking group it controls, this year. A move last year to sell CIC was scrapped after it drew political opposition and only two bids that were judged too low.

An early privatisation of GAN is seen as a pre-condition for the European Commission to approve of the aid. The commission has already voiced strong reservations about the amount of French help to faltering state companies. The Commission announced on Friday it would investigate the new rescue plan.

Speculation has resurfaced in the stock market recently that consolidation in the insurance sector could mean more mergers. Some traders have suggested the possibility of a bid for GAN by rival private French insurer AGF, but analysts said it was impossible yet to put a value on GAN.

The rescue plan calls for the state to inject 11 billion francs in capital in 1997 and give guarantees against future losses in GAN's property portfolio estimated at nine billion francs. The new money comes on top of 2.9 billon francs in state aid already funnelled into the company in 1995.
The payout could be more as the state has agreed to underwrite any future losses tied to GAN's real estate arm UIC.

Out of the rescue money, some seven billion francs will go to cover losses at GAN's UIC property unit which has run up losses of 30 billion francs in three years and 3.9 billion francs for GAN Assurances, hit by poor underwriting results.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis has said the GAN bailout will not endanger France's efforts to cut its deficit to meet conditions for qualifying for a single European currency.
The government will find the money from cash from other privatisations carried out in 1996 and 1997.

After the announcement, one Paris brokerage upped its 1997 profit forecast from a loss of 3.3 francs per share to a profit of 15 francs per share. For 1998, it was looking for a profit of 17 francs compared with an earlier estimate of 7.3 francs.
($ = 5.708 French Francs)
